prompt: What does like-for-like growth measure?
hint: Which stores are in the sum, and which are left out?

choices.text: The growth of every store and the online shop together, compared with the year before
choices.why: That is total growth, the number the lesson says can be moved by a store that was not open all year.

choices.text: The growth of the stores that traded for the whole of both periods
choices.why: Right: comparing like with like takes a new store's first year and a closed store's absence out of the figure.

choices.text: The growth of the largest store
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; Contagem is the largest and is one of eight comparable stores.

choices.text: Sales per square metre this year against last
choices.why: Sales per m² is a separate indicator (lesson 2); like-for-like is about which stores are counted, not how sales are divided.

prompt: Varanda's stores grew 5.7% in 2025. How many of those percentage points came from Ipatinga, the store that opened in July 2024? Round to one decimal.
hint: Ipatinga's extra sales over the 2024 total of all stores: (7040 − 3350) ÷ 77950 × 100.

prompt: In the sheet, Ipatinga's growth comes out at 110.1%. Why does the lesson keep it out of any ranking of stores?
hint: How many months does each year of Ipatinga cover?

choices.text: Because a growth above 100% is a spreadsheet error
choices.why: Growth above 100% is perfectly possible; the formula is right and the comparison is what is wrong.

choices.text: Because Ipatinga is the smallest store
choices.why: It is not the smallest, and size would not exclude it; Sete Lagoas and Divinópolis sell less and are ranked.

choices.text: Because a new store's sales are recorded in a different system for its first year, so they cannot be trusted
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about a separate system; the numbers are fine, and they measure different lengths of time.

choices.text: Because it compares a full year with six months
choices.why: Right: the store opened in July 2024, so its 'growth' measures the calendar, not its selling.

prompt: Varanda is writing its rule for which stores count as comparable. Which of these cases does the rule have to settle? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that changes how long, or where, a store traded.

choices.text: Betim closes for six weeks of refurbishment in 2026
choices.why: Right: six weeks shut make that year shorter for Betim, and the rule says whether it stays in.

choices.text: Sete Lagoas moves to a larger building nearby
choices.why: Right: a bigger store in a new place is arguably a new store, and the rule has to say which.

choices.text: Contagem's sales fall 1.3% against the year before
choices.why: A fall is a result, not a reason to drop a store; leaving out the stores that shrink would flatter the figure.

choices.text: One of the two years being compared is a leap year
choices.why: Right: 2024 had one more trading day than 2025, and the rule says whether to adjust for it.

choices.text: Savassi's manager is replaced in the middle of the year
choices.why: A new manager does not change how long the store traded; it stays comparable.

prompt: Why does a stock-out not show up as low sales in Varanda's sales data?
hint: What does the till record?

choices.text: The till records only what was sold, so a customer who found the hook empty leaves no record
choices.why: Right: the sale that did not happen is recorded nowhere, which is retail's odd property.

choices.text: The stock system deletes the product's sales while it is out
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; there is simply nothing to record.

choices.text: Stock-outs are counted as returns
choices.why: A return is a sale reversed; a stock-out is a sale that never existed.

choices.text: The buyer corrects the sales figure by hand
choices.why: Nobody adds the missing sales back; that is exactly why the lesson estimates them.

prompt: Potting soil sold 360 bags in the 25 days it was on the shelf and was out for the other 3 of the 28. Estimate the bags lost, rounded to a whole number.
hint: The daily rate on days in stock, times the days out.

prompt: The hose reel's sell-through for the four weeks was 100%. What does that tell the buyer?
hint: Look at its stock on hand and its days in stock.

choices.text: That the reel is the category's best performer and needs no action
choices.why: The lesson calls it the best-looking result and the worst one: the reel ran out.

choices.text: That the price is too low
choices.why: Nothing in the data is about price; the reel sold at its normal rate until there were none.

choices.text: That every unit sold and the shelf then stood empty
choices.why: Right: 0 on hand and 10 days out of stock; 100% here is a stock-out, not a triumph.

choices.text: That the supplier delivered more than ordered, so all of it sold at once
choices.why: The supplier's orders are in the next section, and the late one explains the empty shelf, not an extra delivery.

prompt: Next September, Varanda orders hose reels using a forecast built from 2025's sales by week. What does the lesson expect that forecast to get wrong?
hint: What do ten days with no stock look like in a sales history?

choices.text: It will get it right, since a forecast built on a whole year of real sales includes that year's effects
choices.why: The history includes the stock-out as if it were the customers' choice, which is the problem.

choices.text: It will order too many, because the 100% sell-through looks like strong demand
choices.why: A forecast from sales counts units sold, and the empty days add none.

choices.text: It will be right in October and wrong in December
choices.why: The ten empty days were in October, so October is where the history is short.

choices.text: It will order too few, because the empty days read as weak demand
choices.why: Right: it learns that reels do not sell in October, orders fewer, and the shelf empties sooner.

prompt: In Renata's spring campaign, what was the holdout?
hint: Ten per cent of the list.

choices.text: 4,000 customers drawn at random who received nothing
choices.why: Right: what they bought is the estimate of what the others would have bought without the campaign.

choices.text: The customers who had not bought for a year, left out because they would not answer
choices.why: That is the biased choice the lesson warns against: such a group buys less for its own reasons.

choices.text: The customers who opened the email but did not use the coupon
choices.why: They received the campaign, so they cannot show what happens without it.

choices.text: Last spring's customers, used for comparison
choices.why: A different year differs in weather, prices and much else; the holdout is the same weeks, the same list.

prompt: A later campaign goes to 50,000 customers, who place 1,500 orders; a random holdout of 5,000 places 130. How many orders did the campaign add?
hint: The difference in the two rates, applied to the 50,000.

prompt: Why did the spring campaign cost R$ 312 per order it caused, when the report said R$ 59 per order?
hint: Who received the discount, and how many of them needed it?

choices.text: Sending three emails to 36,000 customers cost far more than the budget had allowed for
choices.why: Sending was R$ 3,600 of R$ 89,784; the discount is the cost that matters.

choices.text: The holdout's purchases were counted as campaign cost
choices.why: The holdout received no coupon, so it cost nothing.

choices.text: Only 288 of the 1,512 discounted orders would not have happened anyway
choices.why: Right: R$ 89,784 over 288 incremental orders; the other 1,224 would have come anyway, at full price.

choices.text: The average ticket fell during the campaign
choices.why: The sheet uses the same R$ 380 throughout; the gap comes from the denominator.

prompt: The sales a campaign added over what would have happened without it are measured by its ___.
hint: The lesson's word for it.

prompt: Of the supplier's eight purchase orders, what percentage arrived both complete and on time?
hint: Count the orders where In full and On time are both 1.

prompt: The same eight orders give a fill rate of 98.3% and an OTIF of 37.5%. Which explanation is right?
hint: What does each one count?

choices.text: One of the two was computed wrongly
choices.why: Both are correct; the lesson computes both from the same table.

choices.text: Fill rate counts units and ignores dates; OTIF counts orders that were complete and on time
choices.why: Right: six missing reels in 1,080 barely move the first, while five failed orders in eight sink the second.

choices.text: Fill rate is measured by the supplier, so it is less accurate
choices.why: Lívia computed both from Varanda's own ERP; the difference is what they count, not who counts.

choices.text: OTIF also counts the units lost on the shelf
choices.why: OTIF is about the supplier's orders; the lost sales come from the stock page.

prompt: A delivery reaches the Contagem warehouse on Friday evening, on its promised date, and is checked in on Monday. If OTIF is computed from the goods receipt's date, what happens?
hint: Whose date is the receipt's date?

choices.text: The supplier is scored three days late for Varanda's own weekend
choices.why: Right: the receipt records when somebody typed it, so the rule must say which date counts.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the ERP stores the time the truck arrived at the gate
choices.why: The lesson says the receipt's date is the day it was typed, not the day the truck came.

choices.text: The order counts as not in full
choices.why: Every unit arrived; the date is the problem, not the quantity.

choices.text: The fill rate falls by three per cent
choices.why: Fill rate ignores dates altogether.

prompt: The supplier's average delay was under two days, yet one order nine days late emptied the shelf. What does the lesson say the reorder rule needs to know?
hint: Lesson 9's reorder point used the lead time.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the average, which is what the reorder point already uses
choices.why: The average hid the nine-day order; that is the lesson's point.

choices.text: The supplier's fill rate
choices.why: At 98.3% it said nothing about the late order.

choices.text: The price of the reel
choices.why: Price sets the cost of the lost sales, not how much safety stock the delay calls for.

choices.text: How much the lead time varies, not only its average
choices.why: Right: a lead time that is sometimes nine days late needs more safety stock than its mean suggests.

prompt: Match each retail indicator to what it divides.
hint: Units, orders, days.

pairs.right: Orders complete and on time ÷ all orders
Units on hand ÷ units sold per day in stock

prompt: Put the steps of measuring a campaign's effect in order.
hint: The comparison has to exist before anything is sent.
items: Draw a random holdout from the list
Send the campaign to everybody else
Count each group's orders over the same weeks
Apply the difference in rates to the campaign group
Divide the campaign's cost by the incremental orders
trap: Choosing the holdout after the campaign, from whoever did not answer, measures who answers, not what the campaign did.

prompt: Lesson 17's trap for retail is crediting growth to the wrong cause. Which of these fall into it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where did the extra sales really come from in each case?

choices.text: Praising the store managers for 5.7% growth when 4.7 points came from a new store
choices.why: Right: like-for-like growth was 1.0%.

choices.text: Reporting 1,512 campaign orders as the campaign's result
choices.why: Right: the holdout shows 1,224 of them would have come anyway.

choices.text: Estimating the sales lost while the hose reel was out of stock
choices.why: That is the opposite move: putting a number on a loss the data hides, with its assumption written beside it.

choices.text: Scoring the supplier on OTIF rather than on fill rate
choices.why: That is a choice of indicator, and the better one for a shelf that must not be empty.

prompt: Asked of retail, what is the answer to lesson 17's question about the data and what is odd about it?
hint: The receipt and the empty hook.

choices.text: Retail data is too small to analyse without sampling
choices.why: Retail records every item sold; size is not its problem.

choices.text: Sales are recorded once a month, at the close
choices.why: The till records each sale as it happens, to the minute.

choices.text: Each sale is recorded to the item and minute, and a sale that did not happen leaves no trace
choices.why: Right: complete records of what happened, and nothing about the customer who left empty-handed.

choices.text: Customers' names are attached to every receipt
choices.why: Many store receipts carry no name at all; that is not what the lesson singles out.

prompt: Growth measured only over the shops that traded for the whole of both periods is called ___ growth.
hint: Comparing like with like.
